transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Evelyn Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (NorthStar CTO), Oliver Reyes (ML Eng), Priya Kapoor (SRE), Rajiv Singh (Product)

Summary (auto):
- Week 3 POC sync focused on latency/throughput results vs their incumbent baseline (LexaAI).
- Reviewed tuned configs from Redwood lab (continuous batching + prefix cache + int8 quant path).
- Identified mismatch in load profile for baseline runs; agreed to rerun with identical 95th percentile concurrency script.
- Next steps: share raw logs, security pack, schedule infra deep dive.

Topics: latency distribution, p95/p99 analysis, throughput drop at scale, batching window, KV cache priming, quantization tradeoffs, PCI private deployment concerns.

[00:00] Evelyn: ok everyone thanks for joining, I'll kick off quick — we good on audio?
[00:12] Maya: yeah, we can hear you, thanks.
[00:15] Evelyn: quick agenda — recap last week, Samir will run through the bench slides, then open for q's and next steps.
[00:28] Rajiv: sounds good.
[01:02] Samir: cool, so I pasted the lab sheet link in the chat, link is /sheets/northstar-2025-10-bench (see chat). I'm going to share my screen — oh actually, dropping main numbers here: median latency for our 8k-context model variant is 78ms, p95 is 210ms, p99 around 420ms under the target load. Throughput sustained about 180 req/sec per pod in the config we used. Baseline LexaAI numbers they provided last week were median 95ms, p95 270ms, p99 580ms but caveat: their baseline run used a 2x concurrency profile which we think inflated tail.
[02:00] Oliver: quick question, are those numbers for hosted Redwood or dedicated instance?
[02:07] Samir: those are hosted cluster runs in our lab that mimic your environment with the same instance type ("A100-ish" equivalence), but not the customer-dedicated pool — we also ran a dedicated sim which is in the detail tab.
[02:25] Maya: when you say "A100-ish" — you mean the same GPU family we have in our baseline infra? Lexa had a mix, we weren't sure if configs matched.
[02:36] Samir: yeah sorry, we tried to match GPU family and memory footprint; there might be slight diff in driver/kernel combo — we noted kernel flags. That's actually one reason to run identical baseline script we asked for.
[02:52] Priya: also SRE notes — NV switch interconnect differences can change KV cache pressure, that might be hitting tails.
[03:10] Evelyn: good point. Samir, can you explain the "KV cash" priming — I heard it wrong last week in the notes.
[03:19] Samir: ha, yeah 'K-V cash' — so we do prefix KV cache priming, meaning warm the key-value cache for common prefixes, which reduces first-token overhead for long-context sessions. In our runs we ran two modes: cold-start (no priming) and warm-start (primed). The warm-start improves p95 by ~40ms in our tests.
[03:45] Maya: is priming something we'd be able to do in-prod with the privacy constraints? we can't store customer text, it's sensitive.
[03:53] Samir: priming is config based — you can use synthetic prefix templates derived from your prompt distribution; it's not necessary to store PII. Also we support TTLs and encrypted storage via your KMS.
[04:05] Oliver: and quant path — you mentioned int8 / int4 pipelines, what's the quality delta?
[04:12] Samir: we ran int8 with per-channel calibration, BLEU/ROUGE-style evals on your eval set show <0.8% delta on generation metrics for our target prompts. There are edge cases — longer reasoning chains sometimes drift; we flagged those in the eval tab.
[04:33] Rajiv: so cost v.s accuracy — I assume quant saves tokens GPU time, but does that change latency?
[04:39] Samir: quant typically reduces latency per token due to faster matmuls and cache fits, so yes it helps latency and throughput. But switching to int4 may require different kernel selection and some models need extra tuning.
[04:55] [05:00] Maya: ok let's look at tail behavior — you have a graph for p99 vs concurrency?
[05:05] Samir: yes. On the graph: below 200 concurrent sessions p99 is ~430ms, but once we push to 450 concurrent it climbs to above 700ms due to queuing in the batching layer and occasional hot KV eviction. We can mitigate that with a lower max batch window and tighter flow-control.
[05:28] Priya: do you throttle per token or per request? our SRE needs deterministic SLOs not probabilistic.
[05:36] Samir: we can enforce per-request token limits and hard concurrency caps, plus soft prioritization for critical routes. It does add cost if you need reserved capacity.
[05:50] Evelyn: Maya, what are your SLO targets again for p95/p99?
[05:54] Maya: p95 <250ms, p99 <600ms ideally for user-facing inference. Background batch can be looser.
[06:02] Evelyn: cool — on the numbers we reported, hosted Redwood warm-start p95 210ms so we're within p95 target; p99 is borderline but tunable.
[06:15] Oliver: the baseline Lexa p99 580ms was from their vendor whitebox but they used a shorter tail window — I think it's not apples-to-apples.
[06:28] Samir: yep that's the mismatch we called out — their concurrency pattern bursts in a different way. We suggested running a 95th percentile identical load (script we provided) so both sides use the same profile.
[06:40] Maya: I want to call out an observation from our product team: under medium bursts we saw slight hallucination increase in a specific prompt category when using aggressive quant — likely due to attention kernel selection. Can you add that to the eval notes?
[06:58] Samir: noted — added comment. We'll include raw token logs and the attention maps for the flagged prompts.
[07:12] Rajiv: any infra-level change if we go dedicated? Does that affect tail?
[07:18] Samir: dedicated pools give you pinned GPUs and control over colocations, which reduces noisy neighbor and can flatten tails. Also you can choose reserved capacity with burst, so you get consistent p99. But cost is higher.
[07:34] Maya: Priya, are there network constraints on your side that might add 50-100ms?
[07:40] Priya: our average intra-VPC RTT to their test env was ~12ms, but we have a NAT gateway that sometimes spikes — we can run tests in a debug VPC to remove NAT.
[07:52] [08:00] Oliver: can you walk through the kernel flags you used? we need kernel/driver parity to believe the comparisons.
[08:06] Samir: sure — main flags: CUDA 12.x, cuDNN 9.x, and we used mixed-fp16 matmul with int8 quant fallback. Also tuned gemm split size and used our optimized attention kernel when sequence length > 4k. This is all recorded in the infra tab.
[08:36] Maya: Sequence length >4k — are you seeing any spikes when sequence crosses that threshold?
[08:41] Samir: yes, memory fragmentation and KV GC can cause short lat spikes. We recommend batching windows that are sequence-length aware.
[08:55] Evelyn: quick pause for questions — anybody from NorthStar want to chime in on business side?
[09:02] Rajiv: timeline question — if we need to go dedicated, what's lead time?
[09:07] Samir: reserved Dedicated pools typical lead is 3-4 weeks after contract; for pilot we can allocate a small dedicated slice faster if you commit to a short-term reserved window.
[09:18] Maya: and compliance — do you have SOC2 + ISO packages we can share with procurement?
[09:23] Evelyn: yes, I'll send the packet after the call, and our CSM can open an Entitlements checklist; you asked about private deployment options — we have VPC and on-prem packages, Priya.
[09:36] Priya: on-prem is interesting but we need to see install automation, e2e tests, and KMS integration.
[09:44] Samir: we have an on-prem installer and a private control plane option; we'll include the deployment guide in the security bundle.
[09:56] [10:00] Maya: let's go back to the raw bench comparison — can you talk about batching strategy you used?
[10:05] Samir: we used continuous batching with a 12ms micro-batch window and dynamic batching cap of 64 tokens per batch. For longer sequences we drop the window to 6ms to reduce tail. There's a trade-off: smaller windows reduce tail but lower throughput.
[10:24] Oliver: do you expose a knob for primality of KV priming? like how to pick prefixes?
[10:29] Samir: we provide a template-based priming config, you can upload distribution histograms and we generate synthetic prefixes; also TTLs and non-PII mode.
[10:40] Rajiv: any cost numbers associated with the different configs?
[10:44] Evelyn: yes, we put cost delta estimates in the sheet — roughly, warm-start + int8 saves ~22% token compute cost vs cold fp16 on our test workload. Dedicated reserved gives lower per-token but fixed monthly.
[10:58] Maya: can you show a concrete scenario where cost and latency meet our target?
[11:02] Samir: scenario A (hosted warm-start + int8): p95 ~210ms, throughput 180 rps, est cost $0.045 per 1k tokens. Scenario B (dedicated reserved + warm-start): p95 ~190ms, p99 ~510ms, throughput 220 rps, est cost $0.038 per 1k tokens but + reservation fee.
[11:28] Priya: those numbers look promising; we need to validate p99 during our 95th profile.
[11:34] [12:00] Oliver: let's surface a gotcha — your lab runs show a transient GC pause at ~23 minutes into a sustained run; is that expected?
[12:09] Samir: that was an artifact of our auto-memory compaction policy aligned with long sequence churn. We've since patched the compaction schedule; new run removed that pause. We'll attach both traces.
[12:26] Maya: good. On the baseline side, we saw a different behavior: Lexa did a shorter run and had no tail spike but their load wasn't sustained.
[12:38] Evelyn: okay can we agree to re-run Lexa and Redwood with the same 30-minute sustained profile at 300 concurrency?
[12:45] Maya: yes, we'll coordinate and Oliver will re-run Lexa test.
[12:49] Oliver: noted.
[12:53] [13:00] Rajiv: procurement question — if we switch to dedicated mid-pilot, how does billing pro-rate?
[13:05] Evelyn: typically we pro-rate the first month and issue a credit for unused hosted usage; we'll have finance detail in the commercial packet.
[13:12] Priya: security — can you do a live pen test on private deployment?
[13:17] Samir: we support customer-led pen tests; we provide test scopes and an SOW.
[13:24] Maya: any additional telemetry we can get? trace-level per-token timing?
[13:29] Samir: yes we can provide per-token traces, token-level latencies, and kernel-level breakdowns; those are large files but we'll share them.
[13:41] [14:00] Rajiv: we need a clear decision point — after the rerun and shared logs we'll decide whether to expand pilot. What's a sensible cutover criteria?
[14:49] Maya: if p95 across the sustained run remains <250ms and p99 <600ms and hallucination delta <1% on our eval set, we move to phase 2 (dedicated trial).
[15:00] Evelyn: sounds reasonable. We'll capture that as acceptance criteria.
[15:05] Samir: one more technical note — we noticed their baseline had a different batching strategy that favored throughput over latency; if they tune to latency their throughput drops significantly, so it's important tests match.
[15:22] Priya: any chance to do an A/B where half traffic to Redwood and half to baseline for a small user cohort?
[15:28] Maya: good idea, but we need to be careful about user-facing regressions. Maybe a shadow traffic run first.
[15:36] Samir: we can do shadowing and traffic shifting via rollouts; Redwood Console supports that.
[15:42] Rajiv: we also want cost forecasting for a 10M monthly token volume scenario.
[15:47] Evelyn: we'll produce a cost projection table with range low/med/high and include token mix assumptions.
[15:54] [16:00] Oliver: last technical ask — can you give us the exact micro-batching window config and the flow-control backpressure thresholds? our SRE needs to replicate.
[16:09] Samir: yes I'll include them in Samir-config.txt in the sheet.
[16:15] Maya: great. Any blockers?
[16:19] Priya: we need penetration test scope and KMS walkthrough.
[16:23] Evelyn: noted, included in next steps.
[16:27] [17:00] Maya: quick nit — on the hallucination metric, you said <1% but some of our prompts are multi-turn with system prompts; is that accounted for?
[17:36] Samir: we tested both single-turn and multi-turn; the multi-turn had slightly higher drift under aggressive quant. We'll surface per-prompt breakdowns.
[17:48] Rajiv: timeline recap?
[17:52] Evelyn: action items we've listed in the sheet: 1) Redwood sends security packet + private deploy guide by 10/16, 2) Samir pushes tuned config and kernel flags by 10/18, 3) NorthStar re-runs baseline with identical 30-min profile and uploads traces by 10/20.
[18:12] Maya: ok we're aligned.
[18:16] Evelyn: any other questions?
[18:19] Oliver: none from me.
[18:22] Priya: all good.
[18:25] Rajiv: thanks everyone.
[18:29] Evelyn: thanks, we’ll follow up in the sheet and schedule the deep dive for week of 10/22.
[18:34] Maya: bye all.

End of transcript.
